author: Bob Clausen
title: Arkansas Attorney General's Office, advocates work to rescue women swept up in human trafficking epidemic - NewsBreak
text:
By Bob Clausen ,
55 minutes ago
The Arkansas Attorney General’s office has not tried to hide the fact that they are steamrolling illegal massage parlors in Arkansas, but after the search warrants, the arrests, and seizure of evidence, they discovered a humanitarian aspect they could not walk away from.
“I did not realize what I was going to discover,” Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said.
Department of Public Safety & Arkansas State Police launch statewide webpage to provide resources for human trafficking victims It is a human element, not criminal, but crying out for help.
“If you have been persuaded with false promises, forced, threatened, or hurt to work in a massage business, you are not alone. You deserve to be safe and free.”
That is part of a message of hope a translator offers to the women brought to the U.S. and caught in a world they feel they can’t escape.
“We have been in awe of the sheer magnitude of the issue. Not just in our state but around the nation, of how many women are involved in this,” said Gretchen Smeltzer with Into Light a victims’ advocacy group, helping these women.
Attorney General Tim Griffen said there is a glaring common denominator: These places are connected to each other and directly to mainland China.
“There’s Chinese currency and wire transfers to China,” Griffin said.
And China provides the number one and most valuable resource for every one of them, young women.
“They want the American dream. They are told in China they are going to get to come here make a living. They can send money home, support family, and they are hopeful of that.” Smeltzer said.
But their hope turns to a living hell.
“They’re put into sex slavery,” Griffin said.
Arkansas Attorney General announces grant to combat human trafficking in Arkansas “They’re living in these parlors 24/7, working from 9 in the morning to 10 at night, 7 days a week,” Smeltzer added.
Wayne Bewley, the Attorney General’s Chief Investigator, said the conversation began early on when massage parlors came into focus. He and Griffin agreed the young women involved were far from guilty of a crime and in need of help.
“These massage parlors, they were going in and arresting the girls in the business. What we learned in doing that, you’re arresting the victims and allowing those committing human trafficking to walk free,” Bewley said.
Now, when arrests are made, like that of Gary Liu, who is being held on a $10 million bond in Arkansas, authorities take a different approach with the women involved.
“We’re attacking it in a totally different way at this point, realizing they are in fact victims of human trafficking,” Bewley said.
Arkansas State Police announce results of human trafficking operation in Fort Smith Interpreters are brought in to explain that there is help for them, in hopes of turning them away from the people trafficking them, because often they hide in the darkness and may just move on to another similar situation.
“They think, ‘Oh no, they are in trouble.’ There is a lot of shame connected with this situation.”
When they get a clear picture that help is at hand, fears of what they may have been told about reaching out for help here are eased, and hope is renewed. Bewley said the raids and outreach go hand in hand now.
“When we show up and have victim services, nurses offering medical, it gives us credibility that we are truly looking out for their best interest and not just attempting to put them in jail,” he said.
Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin announces state-wide human trafficking investigation and raid Smeltzer said these women are literally coming out of the darkness and into the light. Explaining one encounter.
“The woman’s face was just beaming. Full of joy, she said, ‘I’m so happy, I’m so happy.’ She was not worried about what she was going to be doing that day. She was able to just be-was able to cook for the women she was living with,” Smeltzer said. “It’s a blessing to see the joy and just peace she has been able to get out of this.”
One desired result yes, But Griffen says make no mistake, he’s learned from talking with others involved why these parlors are so prevalent in our state and country. Why mainland China turns a blind eye to the abuse of their own young woman, because there’s far more at stake.
Griffin travels the country and shares with other agencies how Arkansas is attacking the problem and it’s catching on.
